output.summary: Prior antibiotic exposure can reduce CSF culture sensitivity and Gram stain positivity in bacterial meningitis while leaving CSF chemistries (protein, glucose, lactate) and cell counts abnormal. CSF bacterial antigen testing (latex agglutination) and meningitis/encephalitis multiplex PCR panels remain positive despite antibiotic pretreatment and can aid diagnosis in culture-negative cases. Serum procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL and CSF lactate >3.5 mmol/L have been studied as aids in distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis when CSF findings are equivocal. Empiric antibiotic regimens and adjunctive dexamethasone for adult bacterial meningitis follow standard IDSA/ESCMID guidelines.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Recognise functional asplenia and ensure coverage of encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae); arrange post-recovery vaccination per ACIP.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.

Asplenia (anatomic or functional) dramatically increases risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae); these patients require lifelong vaccination and a low threshold for empiric antibiotics.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Shanice Washington is a 42-year-old right-handed woman with a history of splenectomy following a motor vehicle accident at age 32, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and recurrent sinusitis who presents to the emergency department with worsening headache, confusion, and fever. Her wife provides the majority of the history as the patient is intermittently confused. She reports that approximately four days ago, she developed nasal congestion, mild headache, and a temperature of 100.2°F. She was seen by her primary care physician the following day, who diagnosed sinusitis and started amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily. For the first two days on antibiotics, her symptoms seemed to plateau — the congestion improved slightly but the headache persisted and she developed intermittent chills. Yesterday evening, her wife noticed she seemed 'not herself,' describing her as slow to answer questions and somewhat disoriented when she got up to use the bathroom, bumping into the doorframe. She attributed this to fatigue and a possible reaction to the antibiotics. This morning, she found her in bed complaining of a severe headache that she rated as 9 out of 10, far worse than anything she had experienced before. She was photophobic, wincing when she opened the blinds, and when she asked her what day it was, she gave the wrong answer. She vomited once while getting dressed. Her temperature at home was 100.8°F. She immediately drove her to the emergency department, arriving at 08:45. In the ED, she reports the headache as predominantly frontal and occipital, constant, and throbbing. She denies any visual changes, weakness, or numbness in her extremities. She has no history of seizures and no witnessed seizure activity. Her wife reports she has not traveled recently, has no known sick contacts other than a student with a cold two weeks ago, and has not had any recent dental procedures. She also notes that she missed her follow-up appointment for pneumococcal vaccine booster that was recommended by her hematologist two years ago.
